title: Hexadecimal
intro: Catch up with the essential learning in about 10–15 minutes. Complete five short steps and check your answers as you go.

stages.label: Remember
stages.lead: Retrieve binary addition and shifting from Lesson 002.

questions.prompt: Add 00001011 and 00000110. Give the denary total.
Shift unsigned 00110001 left by one bit. What eight-bit binary result do you get?
questions.feedback: The bit pattern moves left, filling zero on the right.

stages.label: Learn
stages.lead: Understand hexadecimal and how it relates to binary.

blocks.title: Hexadecimal is base 16
blocks.text: Hex uses digits 0–9 then letters A, B, C, D, E and F for values 10–15. One hexadecimal digit represents four binary bits (a nibble), and two hexadecimal digits represent one byte.

blocks.title: Binary to hexadecimal
blocks.text: Split the eight bits into two groups of four; convert each group using its place values 8, 4, 2, 1. For example 1100 | 0111 becomes C7, because 1100 is 12 and 0111 is 7.

blocks.title: Hexadecimal to denary
blocks.text: A3 = (10 × 16) + 3 = 163. The left hexadecimal digit counts multiples of sixteen.

blocks.title: Real-world use · colours
blocks.text: A screen colour may be written as #00FF00. The pairs give red 00, green FF, blue 00. Hexadecimal is shorter to read than long binary but it does not reduce stored bits.

questions.prompt: How many binary bits correspond to one hexadecimal digit?
questions.feedback: Four bits (one nibble) correspond to one hexadecimal digit.

questions.prompt: How many hexadecimal digits represent one eight-bit byte?
questions.feedback: Eight bits contain two four-bit nibbles; each nibble is one hex digit.

stages.label: Practise
stages.lead: Match nibble codes and practise conversions.

blocks.text: Four-bit place values are 8, 4, 2 and 1. Each group of four bits becomes one hex digit.

questions.prompt: Match binary nibbles to hexadecimal digits.
Arrange the method for converting eight-bit binary into hexadecimal.
items: Convert each four-bit group to a hex digit
Split into two groups of four bits
Join the hex digits from left to right
answer: Split into two groups of four bits
Convert each four-bit group to a hex digit
Join the hex digits from left to right
questions.feedback: Split into nibbles, convert them separately, then join the two digits.

stages.label: Apply
stages.lead: Code First and explain the usefulness of hex.

blocks.title: Code First · Predict → Write → Test → Improve
blocks.caption: Predict the output. Change the expression to print the value of hexadecimal A3.

blocks.text: Written question: Explain why hexadecimal is useful when people work with binary codes, and why using hex does not reduce the data stored.

questions.prompt: What is hexadecimal A3 in denary?

questions.feedback: (1 × 16) + 14 = 30. The left digit has place value sixteen.

writing.prompt: Explain why people use hexadecimal and how the bits are affected.
writing.model: Hexadecimal represents the same binary data in shorter, easier-to-read notation. Each hexadecimal digit corresponds to four binary bits. A computer still stores those bits; changing the way people write or display the value does not reduce its storage size.
checklist: I explained that hex is shorter or easier to read than long binary strings.
I stated that one hex digit represents four bits.
I explained that the underlying number of stored bits does not change.

stages.label: Check
stages.lead: Check the main misconceptions before finishing.

questions.prompt: One hexadecimal digit represents four binary bits.
questions.feedback: True: one hexadecimal digit corresponds to one nibble.

questions.prompt: The hexadecimal digit E represents denary 15.
Using hexadecimal reduces the number of bits the computer must store.
questions.feedback: False: hexadecimal is an alternate representation, not compression.
